newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Scientists discuss future of Brazil's biodiversity.
newsitem.headline: Scientists discuss future of Brazil's biodiversity.

text.p: Scientists from around the world met on Tuesday to discuss how Brazil might develop the vast but largely untapped natural wealth of its rainforests, highland wildernesses and marine reserves.

"Brazil has a strong role to play in the area of (molecular biology) but it needs a long-term effort to get a structure in place," said Povl Krogsgaard-Larsen of the Royal Danish School of Pharmacy, and one of about 30 experts attending Brazil's first Tropical Molecular Chemistry Workshop.

Since Brazil was discovered by Europeans some 400 years ago, its forests and mineral resources have been stripped, mostly to be exported as raw material. While logging and mining continues, officials were also worried that plants and micro-organisms were being smuggled out for research in overseas laboratories

"The goverment feels it has practically no control over the illegal trade in medicinal plants taken from the Amazon," Wanderley Messias da Costa, director of the government's Amazon Secretariat that organised the workshop, said.

Brazil's biodiversity has long been used for commercial purposes around the world. In the 19th century, for example, seeds of native rubber trees were exported to Asia, where mass farming eventually destroyed Brazil's rubber boom.
Several leading drugs companies use derivatives of curare, a poisonous plant resin applied to arrow tips by Indian hunters, for drugs that relax muscles during surgery.

In an attempt to encourage development of biodiversity within Brazil, the three-day workshop was to produce a blueprint for a new research institute to carry out molecular analysis of species that may have an industrial use.

Costa said a new patents law would encourage laboratories and food companies to invest in the research centre and find new, environmentally sustainable products that would provide an alternative to logging for poor jungle communities.

"Instead of chopping down our trees and ripping up our plants, we should be looking to dismantle the structure of our organisms, which in themselves can be sources of wealth," Mario Palma of Brazil's Sao Paulo State University said.

Palma said he was developing the venom of an Amazonian bird-eating spider, which paralyses its prey, for use in drugs that slow the advance of brain disorders such as Alzheimer's and Parkinson's diseases.
